o: The input encodes a file tree as lines separated by `\n`, where each line's depth is the number of leading tabs. A line containing a dot (`.`) is a file; otherwise it's a directory. We must return the length of the longest absolute path (names joined by `/`) ending at a **file**, or 0 if there are none. In Example 2, the deepest file `file2.ext` sits at depth 3 under `dir/subdir2/subsubdir2`, giving path length 20 + 1 + 9 + 1 + 9 = 32. Constraints (input length ≤ 10^4) mean any linear scan works — we just need to track, for each depth, the accumulated length of the current directory chain. Key detail: when computing a child's path we add `parentLength + 1` for the `/` separator.
k: Depth of an entry equals its number of leading tab characters; entries are visited in DFS preorder, so backtracking to shallower depths happens naturally as we move through lines.
Keep an array `len[d]` = absolute path length of the directory at depth d on the current chain; a child at depth d+1 has path length `len[d] + 1 + nameLength`.
Only lines whose name contains '.' are files and can update the answer; directories only update the chain-length array.

a.i: Process line by line. Maintain `depthLen` where `depthLen[d]` is the total absolute-path length of the entry at depth `d` currently on our chain. When reading an entry at depth `d` with name length `L`, its path length is `(d == 0 ? 0 : depthLen[d-1] + 1) + L`. If it's a file, update the answer; otherwise store it in `depthLen[d]`. Because input is preorder, overwriting `depthLen[d]` correctly discards finished subtrees.
s: For each line, count leading tabs to get depth d and extract the name.
If name contains '.', answer = max(answer, cur); else depthLen[d] = cur.
a.t: O(n) — each character is examined a constant number of times during splitting and per-line processing.
a.sp: O(n) — for the split lines and the depth map (at most O(depth) entries plus split storage).

a.i: Parse the input recursively by depth: read a line at depth d, then keep consuming subsequent lines with depth d+1 as its children. Each node returns the best path length within its subtree; a file contributes its own full path length, a directory contributes parent prefix + '/' + name plus the best of its children. This mirrors building the actual tree without storing it explicitly.
s: Pre-split input into (depth, name) pairs with an index pointer.
Define dfs(d, prefix): read the next entry; if its depth != d, return 0.
If it's a file, consume nothing and return cur; otherwise recurse on children at depth d+1 and return the max result.
Call dfs(0, 0) from the top level.
a.t: O(n) — every line is parsed once and each recursive call consumes exactly one line.
a.sp: O(n) — for the parsed line list plus recursion stack up to O(maxDepth).

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it's shorter, iterative, and directly exploits the preorder property so no explicit tree or recursion is needed. Common pitfalls: forgetting the `+1` for the `/` separator between parent and child; treating a name like `file.ext` inside a directory listing incorrectly (a file never has children, but checking `'.' in name` handles this since valid names contain dots only for files); returning a directory path instead of 0 when no file exists (Example 3); and off-by-one errors when stripping tabs. Edge cases: single root directory (answer 0), deeply nested single file, multiple files at the same depth. Follow-ups might ask to reconstruct the actual longest path string (store parent pointers alongside lengths), handle spaces in names (already fine), or stream the input without splitting (parse char-by-char tracking current depth and name buffer).
